name: Cheonggyecheon Riparian Corridor
tagline: The river that tore through concrete to reclaim its ancient wilderness.
shortStory: During Korea's Joseon Dynasty in 1411, court astrologers called this stream the throat of the Blue Dragon that protected the royal capital. In 1958, modern city developers paved over the entire river under a four-lane highway, suffocating the water in pitch darkness for over 40 years. In 2003, engineers dismantled the highway—and as sunlight struck the ancient riverbed, natural cold springs erupted, and within weeks, wild grey herons, kingfishers, and sparrows returned to bathe right beside pedestrian stepping stones.
overview: A 10.9-kilometre daylighted stream running through central Seoul, the Cheonggyecheon is one of the world's best-known urban river restoration projects. Its narrow riparian corridor now forms a cool, linear refuge for people, birds, fish and insects inside a dense metropolis.
geography: The corridor follows the Cheonggyecheon from Cheonggye Plaza to the Jungnangcheon confluence. It sits in a granite-and-sediment valley below the historic city centre, with stepped embankments, stone weirs and more than twenty bridges.
vegetation: Willows, zelkova, maple and cherry trees line the channel. Reed beds, emergent grasses, mosses and algae grow on the stone bed, while planted islands soften the engineered walls.
ecology: Cold groundwater and treated stream water create a linear microclimate. The water cools nearby streets, supports fish such as sweetfish, and offers nesting and foraging habitat for herons, ducks, sparrows and kingfishers.
threats: Climate stress on shallow urban streams
conservation: The restoration removed an elevated expressway, reopened the channel and reconnected the stream to its catchment. Maintenance now combines water-quality monitoring, habitat planting and careful management of public access.
highlights: An urban river brought back into daylight after decades beneath an expressway.
A documented cooling effect on surrounding city streets during summer.
A living demonstration of how quickly riparian wildlife can recolonise restored habitat.

name: Amazon Basin Rainforest
established: Protected areas established across the basin from the 20th century
tagline: The living lungs of the planet and realm of ancient river spirits.
shortStory: Deep in the flooded igapó swamps, indigenous Tupi tribes speak of Curupira—a spirit with fire-red hair and feet pointed backwards, whose inverted footprints lure greedy poachers into lost anaconda territory. Before tropical storms, elders say you can hear the Curupira knocking on hollow mother trees to test which branches will survive the wind. Beyond the story lies a real forest of staggering complexity: colossal kapok trees, blackwater rivers, jaguars hunting flooded channels and scarlet macaws crossing the sunrise.
overview: The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest and its most extensive river system. It spans nine countries, stores an immense share of Earth's terrestrial carbon and contains roughly one in ten known species.
geography: The basin drains the Andes and the Guiana and Brazilian shields through the Amazon River and more than a thousand tributaries. Seasonal floods create igapó and várzea forests, while upland terra firme forest remains above the flood line.
vegetation: Layered evergreen forest includes giants such as kapok and Brazil nut, palms, lianas, epiphytes and an extraordinary diversity of understorey plants. Flooded forests are adapted to months of inundation.
ecology: The Amazon recycles rainfall, cools the regional climate and exports moisture far beyond its borders. Its rivers and forests support fish, primates, big cats, eagles, insects and fungi in tightly linked food webs.
conservation: A mosaic of national parks, indigenous territories, extractive reserves and transboundary programmes protects large blocks of forest. Effective conservation depends on secure indigenous land rights, fire control and supply-chain accountability.
highlights: Roughly one in ten known species on Earth lives in the Amazon.
Its rivers discharge more water than any other river system on the planet.
Indigenous knowledge and territorial stewardship protect vast areas of intact forest.

name: Yakushima Primeval Cedar Forest
tagline: Where 7,000-year-old cedars whisper to the spirits of the mist.
shortStory: Locals have a saying: 'It rains 35 days a month on Yakushima.' The island's granite peaks wring oceanic typhoons into perpetual mountain mist, feeding ancient cedar trees with resin so dense they refuse to rot for thousands of years. Hidden in Shiratani Unsuikyo stands Jomon Sugi, a colossal cedar estimated to be up to 7,200 years old. Hikers frequently hear wooden tapping sounds echoing from hollow burls—the Kodama tree spirits that inspired Hayao Miyazaki's Princess Mononoke.
overview: Yakushima is a mountainous island where warm ocean moisture meets cool highlands. Its ancient yakusugi cedar forest, moss carpets and cloud-fed streams form one of East Asia's most atmospheric temperate rainforests.
geography: The island rises steeply from the sea to Miyanoura-dake at 1,936 metres. Deep valleys, granite outcrops and fast streams create sharp gradients in rainfall, temperature and soil.
vegetation: Yakusugi cedar, fir, hemlock and broadleaf evergreens form a layered canopy. Bryophytes, ferns and epiphytes coat trunks and rocks, while bamboo grass fills gaps in the understorey.
ecology: Extremely high rainfall and frequent fog sustain a water-rich forest. Fallen logs and deep moss mats store water, and the island's isolation has produced endemic plants, insects and the Yakushima macaque.
threats: Climate change affecting cloud and rainfall patterns
conservation: Most of the island's core forest lies within Yakushima National Park and the UNESCO property. Trails, visitor limits and restoration work protect the most fragile moss and cedar areas.
highlights: Inspiration for Studio Ghibli's Princess Mononoke.
Home to hundreds of bryophyte species and ancient cedar trees.
Cedar resin helps slow decay in the humid, rain-soaked environment.

name: The Black Forest (Schwarzwald)
established: Protected areas designated across the range from the 20th century
tagline: The cradle of fairy tales, phantom lakes, and evergreen mist.
shortStory: When Roman legions first reached the edge of these dense mountains, they halted in awe and named it 'Silva Nigra'—the Black Forest—because silver firs and spruces grew so tightly that daylight vanished. Deep within lies Mummelsee, a pitch-black tarn lake formed in the Ice Age. Folklore tells of the sunken Water King who sleeps beneath the black mirror; disturbing its waters was believed to summon immediate mountain tempests. This enchanted canopy gave birth to the Brothers Grimm's most famous tales.
overview: The Black Forest is a forested mountain range in south-west Germany, famous for dark conifer stands, deep valleys, mineral springs and the cultural landscape that inspired countless fairy tales.
geography: The range runs north-south along the Upper Rhine plain. Its highest point is Feldberg at 1,493 metres. Glacial cirques, waterfalls, steep gorges and high plateaus shape the forest.
vegetation: Silver fir and Norway spruce dominate higher slopes, with beech, oak, maple and ash in mixed stands. Peat bogs, mountain hay meadows and streamside alder add habitat diversity.
ecology: Mosaics of old forest, managed woodland and open meadows support capercaillie, woodpeckers, bats and the returning Eurasian lynx. Streams and bogs regulate water and store carbon.
threats: Spruce dieback after drought and bark beetle outbreaks
conservation: National park and nature reserve designation protects core areas, while rewilding and wildlife corridors help lynx and other species move between forest blocks. Forest management is shifting toward more mixed, climate-resilient stands.
highlights: Landscape inspiration for Hansel and Gretel and Little Red Riding Hood.
Mummelsee's dark colour comes from dissolved organic matter and depth.
Camera-trap evidence shows that Eurasian lynx are breeding in the region again.

name: Redwood Coast & Ancient Groves
established: National park protections from 1968; UNESCO site in 1980
tagline: Cathedral of Earth's living giants touching the sky.
shortStory: Along northern California's rugged coastline, Pacific ocean fog rolls into river valleys every morning. Coast Redwoods have evolved to drink water directly through their needles, allowing them to grow higher than any other organism on Earth. In 2006, naturalists discovered Hyperion—a tree standing 380.1 feet (115.85m) tall, higher than the Statue of Liberty. To protect its shallow roots from crowds, scientists took an unprecedented step: its coordinates were scrubbed from all maps and remain a guarded secret.
overview: The Redwood National and State Parks protect the largest remaining old-growth coast redwood forest. Fog, rivers and ocean influence one of the most productive temperate forests on Earth.
geography: The parks stretch along the northern California coast from Crescent City toward Humboldt Bay. Marine terraces, alluvial flats, steep hillslopes and river valleys support different forest types.
vegetation: Coast redwood dominates the canopy, with Sitka spruce, Douglas-fir, western hemlock and tanoak. Ferns, redwood sorrel and mosses cover the floor; epiphytic plants and salamanders inhabit the canopy and damp understorey.
ecology: Coastal fog supplies summer moisture and moderates temperature. Large trees, fallen logs and dense understorey store carbon and create cool, humid refugia. Salmon-bearing streams link forest and ocean.
conservation: National and state park status protects core groves, while restoration removes old roads, reconnects streams and replants logged areas. Exact locations of exceptional trees are withheld to protect their shallow roots.
highlights: Home to Hyperion, the tallest known living tree at 115.85 metres.
Canopy soils, ferns and salamanders form ecosystems high above the forest floor.
Some coast redwoods have lived for more than 2,000 years.

name: Monteverde Cloud Forest Reserve
tagline: A paradise in the clouds where orchids hang from sky bridges.
shortStory: Perched on the Continental Divide of Costa Rica, trade winds push ocean clouds up the mountains, creating a forest perpetually suspended in mist. This microclimate is home to over 500 orchid species and the legendary Resplendent Quetzal—the sacred emerald bird whose feathers the Maya valued more than gold. In the 1980s, over 1,500 glowing golden toads were spotted mating in misty pools before vanishing without a trace, becoming the mythical ghost of the cloud forest.
overview: Monteverde protects a high-elevation cloud forest on the Continental Divide. Persistent mist, strong winds and cool temperatures create a dense, mossy world with exceptional orchid and bird diversity.
geography: The reserve lies at roughly 1,200–1,800 metres on the Tilarán and Guanacaste ranges. Ridgelines catch moisture-laden Caribbean air, producing clouds, fog and heavy rainfall.
vegetation: Dwarf and wind-shaped trees carry dense epiphyte loads of orchids, bromeliads, ferns and mosses. Taller sheltered valleys contain strangler figs, laurels and mast-producing trees important to frugivores.
ecology: Cloud immersion supplies water directly to epiphytes and keeps humidity high. The reserve is a key stopover and breeding area for birds moving along elevational gradients; its wild avocados sustain quetzals.
threats: Cloud-base rise linked to climate change
conservation: The reserve is privately managed and connected to neighbouring protected areas. Conservation focuses on forest connectivity, watershed protection, careful trail design and long-term biodiversity monitoring.
highlights: More than 500 orchid species have been recorded in the wider reserve.
Suspension bridges let visitors experience the canopy without climbing.
Critical breeding habitat for the Resplendent Quetzal.

In the 1980s, over 1,500 glowing golden toads were spotted mating in misty pools before vanishing without a trace, becoming the mythical ghost of the cloud forest.

Monteverde protects a high-elevation cloud forest on the Continental Divide. Persistent mist, strong winds and cool temperatures create a dense, mossy world with exceptional orchid and bird diversity.

name: Białowieża Primeval Forest
established: Białowieża National Park 1932; UNESCO World Heritage 1979
tagline: Europe's last lowland primeval forest, where deadwood still feeds a lost world.
shortStory: For centuries, Białowieża was a royal hunting preserve, then an imperial estate—an accident of power that kept one of Europe's last lowland old-growth forests standing. Its massive oaks, lime trees and ash rise above a chaos of fallen timber, Fungi recolonise every fallen trunk, and European bison—wiped out in the wild by 1919—were bred back from a handful of zoo animals. Today a transboundary forest on the Polish-Belarusian border shelters lynx, wolves and more than 12,000 animal species.
overview: Białowieża is a vast lowland forest on the Polish-Belarusian border and the best surviving example of the mixed forests that once covered much of Europe. Its ecological value lies as much in deadwood, fungi and invertebrates as in the iconic bison.
geography: The forest occupies a flat to gently undulating plain drained by the Narewka and Leśna rivers. Wet meadows, alder carr, pine stands and rich deciduous forest form a shifting mosaic across the border.
vegetation: Pedunculate oak, small-leaved lime, hornbeam, ash, spruce and alder dominate different habitats. Standing dead trees and fallen logs remain in strict reserves, feeding beetles, fungi and woodpeckers.
ecology: The forest is a reference ecosystem for European lowland woodland. Large carnivores, woodpeckers, rare beetles and fungi depend on old trees, deadwood and natural gaps. Bison act as landscape engineers by browsing and breaking through vegetation.
conservation: The Polish national park, the Belarusian national park and the transboundary UNESCO site protect core areas. Strict protection, expanded buffers and wildlife corridors are central to long-term conservation.
highlights: The largest free-roaming population of European bison lives here.
Ancient oaks and large volumes of deadwood support thousands of species.
It is a key reference site for understanding natural European woodland.

name: Congo Basin Rainforest
country: DR Congo / Republic of Congo / Gabon / Cameroon
established: Protected areas and transboundary reserves established across the basin
tagline: A second lung of the planet, threaded by black rivers and hidden peat.
shortStory: The Congo Basin holds the world's second-largest tropical rainforest, a humid green expanse larger than Western Europe. Its rivers carry some of the darkest water on Earth, stained by tannins from decaying leaves. Forest elephants push through the undergrowth, okapi vanish into bamboo thickets and gorillas build nests in the foliage. Beneath the forest floor, vast peatlands store carbon accumulated over thousands of years—an ecosystem whose value is still being discovered.
overview: The Congo Basin is a mosaic of tropical forest, swamp, river and savanna across six countries. It is the second-largest tropical forest after the Amazon and one of the most important carbon stores on land.
geography: The basin is drained by the Congo River and its tributaries. Vast seasonally flooded forests, swamp forests and terra firme forest sit within a gently undulating landscape, with highlands at the margins.
vegetation: Giant hardwoods, palms, lianas and epiphytes form dense evergreen forest. Gilbertiodendron stands dominate some areas, while river margins support raphia palms and periodically flooded swamp forest.
ecology: Forest elephants are important seed dispersers and disturbance agents. The basin's peatlands hold enormous carbon stocks, while river systems support fish, turtles and aquatic mammals. Great apes, okapi and forest buffalo depend on large intact blocks.
conservation: Transboundary protected landscapes, community forests and international carbon and conservation finance support forest protection. Monitoring is increasingly aided by camera traps, satellite data and local ranger patrols.
highlights: The world's second-largest tropical rainforest.
Vast peatlands store carbon accumulated over millennia.
Forest elephants shape forest structure by dispersing seeds and opening trails.

name: Daintree Rainforest
established: Daintree National Park 1988; UNESCO Wet Tropics 1988
tagline: A living remnant of Gondwana, where cassowaries garden the ancient canopy.
shortStory: The Daintree is one of the oldest continuously surviving rainforests on Earth. Its canopy is a tangle of vines, epiphytes and ancient flowering plant lineages; below it, the Daintree River winds through mangrove and lowland forest to the Great Barrier Reef. Southern cassowaries swallow forest fruit and carry seeds far through the undergrowth, while Boyd's forest dragons sit motionless on mossy trunks. Long isolation has made this a stronghold of endemic species.
overview: The Daintree lies in the Wet Tropics of northern Queensland, where tropical rainforest meets the coast and the Great Barrier Reef. It is renowned for ancient lineages, high endemism and a staggering concentration of primitive flowering plants.
geography: The Daintree River separates the main rainforest block from the coastal lowlands near Cape Tribulation. Steep ranges, gorges, floodplains and mangrove-lined estuaries create a compressed mosaic of habitats.
vegetation: Complex mesophyll and notophyll vine forests form the core canopy, with fan palms, cycads, epiphytes, strangler figs and mangrove forests along the coast. Some plant lineages have persisted for tens of millions of years.
ecology: Cassowaries are keystone seed dispersers. The forest's proximity to the reef means land clearing and runoff can affect both terrestrial and marine systems. Endemic frogs, reptiles, insects and plants are tightly tied to microhabitats.
threats: Runoff affecting the Great Barrier Reef
conservation: The Wet Tropics World Heritage Area, Daintree National Park and Indigenous protected areas safeguard much of the forest. Conservation work focuses on corridors, cassowary road safety and weed control.
highlights: One of the oldest rainforests on Earth, with Gondwanan plant lineages.
A major stronghold of the Southern Cassowary.
The Daintree catchment drains directly into the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area.

name: Sundarbans Mangrove Forest
established: Sundarbans National Park 1984; UNESCO World Heritage 1987
tagline: A drowned forest of tides, roots and swimming tigers.
shortStory: At the mouth of the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers, the Sundarbans rises and falls twice a day beneath enormous tides. Its mangrove roots knit together islands of mud, salt and freshwater, buffering millions of people from cyclones and storm surge. Bengal tigers swim between channels, fishing cats hunt in the reed margins, and spotted deer move through the undergrowth. It is the world's largest mangrove forest and a landscape defined by constant change.
overview: The Sundarbans is a vast tidal mangrove ecosystem shared by Bangladesh and India. It is the world's largest mangrove forest, a UNESCO World Heritage site and a critical coastal defence against cyclones.
geography: The forest occupies the delta of the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers along the Bay of Bengal. Tidal channels, mudflats, islands and saline swamps are reshaped by sediment, storms and changing river flows.
vegetation: Salt-tolerant mangroves such as sundri, gewa, goran and keora dominate. Pneumatophores and stilt roots allow trees to breathe and stabilise soft mud; palms and grasses occupy drier margins.
ecology: Mangroves trap sediment, absorb wave energy and provide nursery habitat for fish and crustaceans. The forest supports Bengal tigers, fishing cats, spotted deer, crocodiles, turtles and migrating birds. Its roots and mud store carbon.
conservation: National parks, tiger reserves, wildlife sanctuaries and Ramsar sites protect the Sundarbans. Management combines anti-poaching patrols, mangrove replanting, cyclone preparedness and community-based resource management.
highlights: The world's largest continuous mangrove forest.
A natural buffer that reduces cyclone and storm-surge impacts.
Bengal tigers here are strong swimmers that regularly cross tidal channels.

myths.title: The Sacred Devarakadus (Groves of the Gods)
myths.story: Scattered across the mountain crests are ancient sacred groves guarded by serpent deities (Nagas). Felling even a single branch was believed to awaken ancestral curses, creating centuries-old pristine ecological sanctuaries that preserved the lion-tailed macaque.
myths.source: Sacred Groves of the Western Ghats / Anthropological Survey of India

myths.story: Legend tells of the goddess Woluo Semo and the mountain god Dage, who gifted her a mirror polished from the wind and sea. When an envious demon startled her, the mirror slipped from her hands and shattered into 108 turquoise and emerald alpine lakes.
myths.source: Tibetan Mountain Legends / Jiuzhaigou National Park Folklore

myths.title: The Sacred Red Cypress of Mount Ali
myths.story: The indigenous Tsou people revere the ancient Taiwan red cypresses (Benihi) as sacred antennas connecting heaven and Earth. When Japanese loggers cut the monumental Sacred Tree, lightning repeatedly struck the mountain railways until peace ceremonies were offered.
myths.source: Tsou Cultural Heritage / Alishan Forest Railway Archives

myths.title: The Lovers of the Cloud Laurel
myths.story: The ancient laurel forest takes its name from princess Gara of La Gomera and prince Jonay of Tenerife. Forbidden from marrying by their families when Mount Teide erupted in fury, the lovers leaped together from the highest misty peak into the laurel canopy below.
myths.source: Guanche Cultural Heritage / Garajonay National Park Records

myths.title: The Place of Darkness (Mubwindi)
myths.story: Bwindi derives from the Runyakitara word 'Mubwindi', meaning 'a dark, impenetrable swamp'. Batwa pygmies believe the forest is alive and sentient; travellers who whisper their true intentions are allowed safe passage beneath the canopy where mountain gorillas nest.
myths.source: Batwa Cultural Experience / Uganda Wildlife Authority

myths.title: Raven and the Releasing of the Sun
myths.story: In Tlingit tradition, the dense temperate rainforest was originally locked in eternal pitch darkness. Raven stole the sun from a greedy chief's cedar box and flew up through the smokehole into the cedar canopy, scattering light into the rivers and spawning salmon.
myths.source: Tlingit Cultural Heritage / Tongass National Forest Archives

myths.title: The Living Fossil of the Secret Canyon
myths.story: For 200 million years, dinosaurs grazed beneath the Wollemi Pine, a tree thought to have been extinct for 65 million years. When park ranger David Noble abseiled into a hidden canyon in 1994, he found fewer than 100 wild trees surviving—a Jurassic oasis hidden in plain sight.

myths.title: Tāne Mahuta, Lord of the Forest
myths.story: In Māori tradition, Tāne Mahuta is the god of forests who pushed apart Ranginui (the Sky Father) and Papatūānuku (the Earth Mother) to let sunlight flood the world. The colossal 2,000-year-old kauri tree in Waipoua is worshipped as the living body of Tāne himself.
myths.source: Māori Oral Traditions / Department of Conservation New Zealand
